chapters.name: Chapter 1: Safe work and finding the fault

lessons.title: Lesson 1: A safe repair bench
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Set up a repair bench that is safe, tidy and ready for work.
This lesson builds toward: Before and during any repair, you will set up a safe bench and handle lithium batteries safely, spotting a swollen, hot or damaged battery, following every rule on your battery safety card.
Your bench is where accidents happen or are prevented. A good bench is dry, well lit, and away from cooking fires, fuel and water. It has a heat-resistant mat, a small tray for screws, and a clear space so tiny parts do not get lost.
Tools: the right screwdrivers, plastic opening tools (spudgers), tweezers, a suction cup, a multimeter, and a hot air tool or soldering iron if you are trained to use them. Heat tools must sit in a stand, never on paper or cloth, and be switched off when you leave the bench.
Protect yourself and the phone: wear safety glasses when you open screens or work with glass, use an anti-static wrist strap or touch bare metal to release static before you touch the board, and keep a metal tin with dry sand near the bench for a damaged battery. Know the way out of your shop and keep it clear.
Step by step:
- Choose a dry, well-lit place away from cooking fires, fuel and water.
- Lay a heat-resistant mat and a screw tray.
- Keep heat tools in a stand and switch them off when you leave.
- Wear safety glasses; release static before touching the board.
- Keep a metal tin of dry sand near the bench and a clear way out.
Words to know:
- Spudger: a plastic tool for opening a phone and lifting parts without scratching or shorting them.
- Multimeter: a tester that measures voltage, current and resistance.
- Static: a small electric charge on your body that can damage a phone's board.
Try it now: Draw a simple plan of your bench (or the bench you want): where each tool goes, where the heat tool stands, where the sand tin is, and the way out. List what you still need to buy.
You can now set up a safe, tidy repair bench with the right tools and safety items.

check.q: Where should a hot air tool sit when you put it down?
options: In its stand, away from cloth and paper
check.why: A stand keeps the hot tip away from things that can burn.

check.q: Why keep a metal tin of dry sand near your bench?
options: To hold a damaged battery safely
check.why: A metal tin of sand is a safer place for a damaged battery than the bench or a bin.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Lithium battery dangers
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot a swollen, hot or damaged battery and handle it without causing a fire.
This lesson builds toward: Before and during any repair, you will set up a safe bench and handle lithium batteries safely, spotting a swollen, hot or damaged battery, following every rule on your battery safety card.
Almost every phone has a lithium-ion battery. It holds a lot of energy. If it is punctured, bent, crushed, overheated or shorted, it can catch fire very fast, give off poisonous smoke, and start burning again after it seems to stop.
Warning signs: swelling (the back cover or screen is lifted), heat, a strange smell, hissing or popping noises, or smoke. A swollen battery must be replaced, never pressed flat, pierced or charged.
Safe habits: disconnect the battery connector first, before you work on the board. Never pry a battery out with a metal tool; use plastic tools and the right adhesive remover, and go slowly. Never use the hot air tool near a battery. Charge phones only with good chargers, on a hard surface, where you can see them.
If a battery starts to smoke or hiss: move people away and do not breathe the smoke. Only if you can do it safely, use long tongs to put it in your metal tin of sand, outside. If there is fire you cannot control, get everyone out and call the fire service.
Step by step:
- Look for swelling, heat, smell, noise or smoke before you open any phone.
- Disconnect the battery before working on the board.
- Use plastic tools, never metal, to remove a battery; never bend or pierce it.
- Keep heat tools away from the battery.
- If it smokes: move people away, use tongs and the sand tin only if safe, call the fire service for a fire.
Words to know:
- Lithium-ion battery: the rechargeable battery in phones; it stores a lot of energy and can burn if damaged.
- Swollen battery: a battery that has puffed up because gas is building inside; it is dangerous.
- Short circuit: when electricity takes a wrong path, for example through a metal tool, causing heat or fire.
Official sources:
- NFPA (US National Fire Protection Association): Lithium-ion battery safety (warning signs; do not put in the trash, recycle)
Try it now: Write your battery safety card in five lines for the wall of your shop: the warning signs, the safe habits, and what to do if a battery smokes. Find out the phone number of your nearest fire service.
You can now spot a dangerous battery, handle batteries safely during a repair, and act safely if one starts to smoke.

check.q: A phone's back cover is lifted because the battery has puffed up. What do you do?
options: Press it flat and close the phone
Pierce it to let the gas out
Replace it, handling it carefully without bending or piercing
check.why: A swollen battery is dangerous; it must be removed carefully and replaced, never pressed, pierced or charged.

check.q: What should you do first before working on a phone's board?
check.why: Disconnecting the battery stops shorts that can damage the board or start a fire.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Finding the fault and writing a job card
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Find the likely fault with a step-by-step check and record the job on a job card.
This lesson builds toward: Given a phone a customer brings in, you will find the likely fault with a step-by-step check and record the job on a job card, with the fault, the agreed price and the customer's consent written before work starts.
Start by listening. Ask the customer what happened: dropped, wet, slow, not charging, no sound? When did it start? Then check from the simplest cause to the hardest. Many "dead" phones only need a good charger, a clean charging port or a software restart.
A simple order: (1) look for damage, swelling or water marks; (2) try a known good charger and cable; (3) clean the charging port gently with a plastic or wooden pick; (4) restart, and check if the problem is software; (5) only then open the phone and test parts.
Before you start any paid work, write a job card and show it to the customer. It records: the date, the customer's name and phone number, the phone model and IMEI, what is wrong, any damage you see (cracks, dents), what you will do, the agreed price, the expected date, and the customer's signature or a recorded "yes". Give the customer a copy or a ticket number. This protects you both.
Example: Kwame in Accra gets a phone that "won't charge". He tries a good cable, cleans lint from the port, and it charges. He charges only a small cleaning fee, and the customer comes back for every repair after that.
Step by step:
- Ask what happened and when it started.
- Look for damage, swelling or water marks.
- Try a known good charger and cable; clean the port gently.
- Restart and check for a software problem.
- Write the job card with the fault, damage seen, price and date, and get the customer's yes before you open the phone.
Words to know:
- Job card: a written record of one repair: the phone, the fault, the price, the date and the customer's agreement.
- IMEI: the phone's unique 15-digit number; dial *#06# to see it.
- Software fault: a problem in the phone's programs, not its parts; often fixed by a restart or update.
Try it now: Draw your own job card on one page with all the boxes from this lesson. Fill it in for a practice phone (yours or a friend's) with a made-up fault.
You can now check a phone from the simplest cause to the hardest and record every job on a job card before you start.

check.q: A customer says the phone won't charge. What do you check first?
options: A known good charger and cable, and a clean port
check.why: Start with the simplest causes; a bad cable or a dirty port is common.

check.q: Why write damage you see, like a cracked corner, on the job card before you start?
options: So no one later blames you for damage that was already there
check.why: Recording existing damage protects you and the customer from disputes.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Running an honest, safe business

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Protecting your customers' data
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Protect each customer's data while their phone is in your shop.
This lesson builds toward: When a customer leaves a phone with you, you will protect the customer's data by asking for a backup and never copying, viewing or sharing their files, never asking for a PIN or password you do not need.
A phone holds a person's life: photos, messages, mobile money, bank apps and contacts. Customers trust you with it. One leaked photo or stolen mobile money balance can destroy your shop's name, and in many countries it can break the law.
Before the repair: ask the customer to back up their phone if they can, and to sign out of mobile money and bank apps or remove the SIM card. Most repairs do not need the phone's lock code. If you truly need it to test the phone, ask the customer to unlock it in front of you, or to set a temporary code and change it after. Never ask for a mobile money or bank PIN. No repair ever needs it.
During and after: do not open photos, messages or apps that are not part of the repair. Do not copy anything, and do not let others handle phones. Store phones in a locked drawer. Shred or keep job cards safely, because they hold names and numbers.
Countries have data protection laws and offices, for example Kenya's Office of the Data Protection Commissioner, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, and Ghana's Data Protection Commission, where businesses that keep personal data must register. Check what your country's office expects from a small business like yours.
Step by step:
- Ask the customer to back up the phone and sign out of money apps, or remove the SIM.
- Do not ask for the lock code unless you truly need it; let the customer unlock it in front of you.
- Never ask for a mobile money or bank PIN.
- Open only what the repair needs; copy nothing.
- Lock phones and job cards away; check your country's data protection rules.
Words to know:
- Personal data: information about a person, such as their name, number, photos and messages.
- Backup: a copy of the phone's data saved somewhere else, so nothing is lost if the repair goes wrong.
- Data protection law: a law that says how businesses must collect, keep and protect people's personal data.
Official sources:
- Office of the Data Protection Commissioner, Kenya
- Nigeria Data Protection Commission (Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023)
- Data Protection Commission Ghana (Data Protection Act, 2012, Act 843; data controllers must register)
Try it now: Write your customer data promise: at least four short lines you will show every customer, such as "We never ask for your mobile money PIN." Write the name of your country's data protection office.
You can now protect your customers' data before, during and after a repair, and know which office sets the rules in your country.

check.q: A technician asks for the customer's mobile money PIN to "test the phone". What is true?
options: It is needed for every repair
It is fine if he is honest
No repair needs it; never ask for it
check.why: No repair ever needs a mobile money or bank PIN.

check.q: What should the customer do before leaving the phone, if they can?
options: Back up the phone and sign out of money apps
check.why: A backup and signing out of money apps protects them if anything goes wrong.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Pricing repairs, warranties and refusing stolen phones
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate a repair price and write a price list with warranty terms.
This lesson builds toward: Given the parts cost and the time a repair takes, you will calculate a repair price and write a price list with warranty terms, covering parts, labour and shop costs with a profit, and a clear warranty. When you have dead batteries, broken screens or a phone you suspect is stolen, you will choose the safe and legal action: store and hand e-waste to a collector, and refuse a phone without proof of ownership, with no burning, no dumping and no buying of phones without proof.
A fair price covers three things and leaves a profit: the part, your time (labour), and a share of your shop costs, such as rent, electricity, tools and data. Example (figures are examples only): a screen costs NGN 15,000. Your labour is NGN 4,000 and your share of shop costs NGN 1,000. Cost: NGN 20,000. Add NGN 3,000 profit: price NGN 23,000.
Parts come in different qualities. Tell the customer honestly which part you are using (original, good copy or cheap copy) and the price of each. A cheap part that fails in a week costs you your name.
A warranty is your promise: if the same repair fails within a set number of days because of your work or the part, you fix it free. Write how many days, and what is not covered (new drops, water, someone else opening the phone). Put the price list and warranty where customers can see them.
Refuse phones that may be stolen. Do not buy, unlock or strip a phone unless the seller shows proof it is theirs, such as the box with a matching IMEI or a receipt. If a phone looks stolen, do not argue; refuse politely. In many countries, buying stolen goods is a crime.
Step by step:
- Add the part cost, your labour and a share of shop costs.
- Add your profit to get the price.
- Offer part choices honestly, with a price for each.
- Write the warranty days and what is not covered.
- Show the price list; refuse phones without proof of ownership.
Words to know:
- Labour: the payment for your time and skill.
- Overhead (shop costs): costs of running the shop, like rent, power, tools and data, shared across jobs.
- Warranty: a written promise to fix the same fault free for a set time.
Try it now: Write your price list for five common repairs: for each, the part cost, labour, shop-cost share, profit, price and warranty days. Use your local currency.
You can now price a repair so it covers all your costs and a profit, write a warranty, and refuse a phone that may be stolen.

check.q: Part GHS 150, labour GHS 60, shop-cost share GHS 20, profit GHS 40. What is the price?
A young man wants to sell you a phone cheaply but has no box and no receipt. What do you do?
options: Buy it fast before others do
check.why: Without proof of ownership the phone may be stolen; refuse.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: E-waste, dead batteries and your shop's starter pack
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Store dead batteries and broken parts safely and hand them to a proper collector.
This lesson builds toward: When you have dead batteries, broken screens or a phone you suspect is stolen, you will choose the safe and legal action: store and hand e-waste to a collector, and refuse a phone without proof of ownership, with no burning, no dumping and no buying of phones without proof. Before and during any repair, you will set up a safe bench and handle lithium batteries safely, spotting a swollen, hot or damaged battery, following every rule on your battery safety card.
Old phones, screens, boards and batteries are electronic waste (e-waste). They contain lead, mercury and other poisons. The WHO says burning e-waste is the most dangerous way to handle it, and harms children and pregnant women most. In 2022 the world made about 62 million tonnes of e-waste, and only 22.3% was documented as properly collected and recycled.
Never burn e-waste to get copper, and never throw batteries in the bin, a fire or a drain. Tape the ends (terminals) of dead batteries, keep them in a closed metal tin of dry sand away from heat, and keep broken screens and boards in a separate labelled box.
Hand them to an e-waste collector or recycler. Ask your county or city council, the environment agency, or phone sellers and network shops which collectors are approved where you are. Keep a note of what you handed over and when.
Now make your starter pack: your price list, your job card, your data promise and your safety card with the battery rules and where your e-waste goes.
Step by step:
- Tape the terminals of dead batteries.
- Keep them in a closed metal tin of dry sand, away from heat.
- Keep broken screens and boards in a labelled box.
- Ask the council or environment agency for an approved collector.
- Hand them over and write down what and when. Never burn or dump e-waste.
Words to know:
- E-waste: old or broken electronic items and parts, such as phones, screens, boards and batteries.
- Terminals: the metal ends of a battery where it connects; taping them stops shorts.
- Recycler: a business that safely takes apart e-waste and recovers materials.
Official sources:
- WHO fact sheet: Electronic waste (e-waste): 62 million tonnes in 2022, 22.3% documented as recycled; dangers of burning
- NFPA (US National Fire Protection Association): Lithium-ion battery safety (warning signs; do not put in the trash, recycle)
Try it now: Make your shop's starter pack, as described in the final task. Add one line to your safety card naming who will collect your e-waste, or the office you will ask.
You can now store and hand over e-waste safely and put together a starter pack for an honest, safe phone repair shop.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Battery safety card No card, or it misses the warning signs or what to do if a battery smokes. The card lists the warning signs, the safe habits and what to do if a battery smokes or burns. It also shows the fire service number and where the sand tin is kept. Job card The job card is missing the fault, the price or the customer's agreement. It records the customer, phone model, IMEI, fault, damage seen, work, price, date and the customer's yes. It also has a ticket number and a box for the warranty end date. Customer data promise No promise, or it asks for a PIN or password. At least four clear lines, including never asking for a money PIN and copying nothing. It also names the country's data protection office and how job cards are kept safe. Price list Prices are guesses, or the arithmetic is wrong. At least five repairs, each with part, labour, shop costs, profit, price and warranty days, adding up correctly. It also shows part choices (original or copy) and what the warranty does not cover. E-waste and stolen phones No plan, or the plan includes burning or dumping. Batteries and parts are stored safely and handed to a named collector or office; phones without proof are refused. It also keeps a record of what was handed over and when. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of your starter pack and try again.

check.q: What is the safest way to get rid of dead phone batteries?
options: Tape the terminals, store them in a sand tin, give them to an approved collector
check.why: Taping, safe storage and an approved collector stop fires and pollution.

check.q: According to the WHO, which is the most dangerous way to handle e-waste?
check.why: The WHO says burning e-waste is the most hazardous practice because of its toxic fumes.
